issues.legal_issue: A tenant who has only applied to purchase land has no vested right that prevents subsequent changes in the landholder’s status from being considered.
material_facts: The tenant applied to purchase the land, but the original landholder was not impleaded in the application.
The original landholder died while the proceedings were pending, and the land passed by inheritance to heirs who were later declared small landholders.
The tenant had not acquired the vested purchase rights that arise after an order in the tenant’s favour and payment of the required first instalment.
The heirs’ rights to the land were also recognized in a civil suit, which declared the alleged transferees to be benamidars and granted the heirs possession.
issues.conclusion: The later change in landholder status had to be considered. The tenant’s application alone created no vested right to purchase, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 18(1) and 18(4)(a)–(b) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a tenant who has only applied to purchase has a mere expectation or liberty to apply, not an accrued right; the court must consider subsequent events and mould relief accordingly. In Rameshwar v. Jot Ram, the tenant had already obtained an order and deposited the first instalment, thereby acquiring a vested right under the legal fiction in Section 18(4)(b), so that decision did not govern this case. The Court applied the principle from Abbot v. Minister for Lands that a mere right to take advantage of an Act’s provisions is not an accrued right.

predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding: A tenant brought a proceeding seeking to purchase land under a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
predicates.application_was_only_a_request: The tenant had applied to purchase but had not yet completed the steps that would vest ownership or a vested purchase right.
predicates.no_vested_purchase_right_before_status_c: No purchase order followed by the required first payment had given the tenant a vested right before the landholder’s status changed.
predicates.landholder_status_changed_during_proceed: The landholder died during the proceeding, and inheritance changed the status of those who held the land.

issues.definition: When a tenant in a purchase proceeding has only applied and has no vested purchase right, a change in the landholder’s status during the proceeding must be considered.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative purchase order does not bind a landholder or heirs who were not parties to the proceeding.
material_facts: The tenant did not implead the original landholder in the purchase application.
After the landholder died, the heirs applied to join the proceeding and were initially added.
The authority later removed the heirs from the proceeding as unnecessary parties and then allowed the tenant’s purchase application.
issues.conclusion: Neither the original landholder nor the heirs were bound by the purchase order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held on these facts that an order made in a proceeding did not bind the original landholder, who had not been impleaded, or the heirs, whose names had been removed from the proceeding before the order was made.

predicates.statutory_purchase_proceeding: A tenant brought a statutory proceeding seeking to purchase land.
predicates.original_landholder_not_joined: The tenant did not make the original landholder a party to the purchase proceeding.
predicates.heirs_removed_before_order: After the landholder died, the heirs were removed from the proceeding before the purchase order was made.

issues.definition: A purchase order does not bind the original landholder or heirs when the landholder was not joined and the heirs were removed before the order.

issues.legal_issue: An oral sale of land does not transfer title when the applicable law requires a registered instrument for the sale.
material_facts: The landholder purported to sell the land orally to two transferees.
The statutory requirement for a registered instrument had been extended to the relevant territory before the purported sales.
The transferees’ names were later entered in mutation records, but the courts found that the purported sales conveyed no title.
issues.conclusion: The alleged oral sales did not pass title to the transferees.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as extended to the relevant territory with effect from April 1, 1955, required a registered instrument for the sales at issue; oral sales could not transfer title.

predicates.land_title_dispute: The proceeding concerned whether a purported transfer conveyed title to land.
predicates.purported_sale_was_oral: The parties relied on an oral transaction as the sale of the land.
predicates.applicable_transfer_law_required_registe: The law applicable to the transaction required a registered instrument to transfer the land by sale.

issues.definition: In a land-title dispute, an oral purported sale conveys no title when the applicable law requires a registered instrument.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal following a judgment that has become final after the dismissal of a challenge to the connected judgment is no longer tenable.
material_facts: The judgment under appeal followed the High Court’s main judgment in connected appeals.
Special leave petitions challenging that main judgment were dismissed in limine.
The High Court had disposed of the appeal at issue in accordance with the main judgment.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was no longer tenable because the connected main judgment had attained finality.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that dismissal of the special leave petitions challenging the connected main judgment left that judgment final and not open to disturbance through an appeal against a judgment that merely followed it.

predicates.appeal_against_judgment_following_connec: A party appealed from a judgment that followed the result in a connected proceeding.
predicates.special_leave_challenge_to_connected_dec: A challenge by special leave to the connected decision had been dismissed.

issues.definition: An appeal from a judgment following a connected decision is no longer tenable when a special-leave challenge to that connected decision has been dismissed.
